d: An almost vertical rock wall on the coast, formed as waves wear away its base and the rock above collapses.
A fast flow of water loaded with mud, rocks and vegetation rushing down ravines, usually after intense rain. It is a major geological hazard in Chile.
A fan-shaped deposit formed where a ravine opens into a wider valley and the flow loses energy.
Extinct marine mollusks with a coiled shell, relatives of today's nautilus. Their fossils help date rocks.
A gray volcanic rock very common in the Andes (hence its name). It forms when lava cools at the surface.
An arch-shaped fold of rock layers (∩). The oldest layers are in the core.
A trough-shaped fold of rock layers (U). The youngest layers are in the core.
A sedimentary rock made of sand grains cemented together over time.
Very old rocks, transformed by heat and pressure, on which younger rocks rest.
A huge body of rock formed by magma that cooled slowly deep in the crust; it can span hundreds of kilometers.
A large fragment of rock or lava thrown out by an explosive eruption.
Mollusks with a two-part shell, like clams and mussels. Their fossils are common in marine rocks.
Marine animals with two shells, similar to bivalves but a different group. They were very abundant in ancient seas.
A large depression formed when a volcano collapses after its magma chamber empties in a huge eruption.
A sedimentary rock made mainly of calcium carbonate, often from the remains of marine organisms.
Tiny fragments of rock and volcanic glass (under 2 mm) blasted out in an eruption; they can travel hundreds of kilometers.
Microorganisms that photosynthesize; they are among the oldest life forms on Earth.
A stream of molten rock moving away from a volcano and solidifying as it cools.
A small cone-shaped volcano built from lava fragments and scoria piled around the vent.
A rounded rock body that grows within a sediment around a nucleus, sometimes a fossil.
A mountain range running parallel to the Chilean coast, lower and older than the Andes.
Geological period from 145 to 66 million years ago. It ended with the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs.
Geological period from 201 to 145 million years ago, a time of great dinosaurs and widespread seas in Chile.
Geological period from 252 to 201 million years ago, when the first dinosaurs appeared.
Geological era from 541 to 252 million years ago, with the first fish, land plants and reptiles.
Geological epoch from 23 to 5.3 million years ago, when much of today's Andes was uplifted.
Geological epoch from 5.3 to 2.6 million years ago.
The epoch of the great ice ages, from 2.6 million to 11,700 years ago. Megafauna lived then.
The current geological epoch, which began about 11,700 years ago at the end of the last ice age.
Geological epoch from 56 to 34 million years ago.
A very hard mineral made of silica; one of the most common in the Earth's crust.
The lower strip of land between the Coastal Range and the Andes, like Chile's central valley.
A sheet of intrusive rock cutting vertically through other rocks; it forms when magma rises through a fracture and cools.
A coarse-grained, dark gray intrusive rock formed by magma that cooled slowly at depth.
Fractures that split rock into columns with 3 to 6 sides (often hexagonal). They form as lava or magma shrinks while cooling, like mud cracking as it dries.
A mound of very viscous lava that piles up over the vent because it cannot flow far.
A pile of sand shaped by the wind. If it no longer receives new sand, it is called a fossil or relict dune.
The wearing away of rocks and soil by water, ice, wind or waves, which also carries the fragments away.
A tall, cone-shaped volcano built of alternating layers of lava and pyroclastic material, like Villarrica or Osorno.
A layer of sedimentary or volcanic rock. As a rule, lower layers are older than upper ones.
Layered structures built by colonies of microorganisms that trap sediment; they have existed for more than 3,500 million years.
A fracture in the crust along which rock blocks have moved relative to each other. Its movement can cause earthquakes.
A group of minerals very common in igneous rocks, white to pink in color.
A very hot, fast avalanche of gas, ash and rock rushing down a volcano's slopes. One of the most dangerous volcanic phenomena.
A turbulent, dilute cloud of gas and ash moving at high speed over the ground.
A body of rock with shared characteristics that can be recognized and mapped; it is named after a place, e.g. the Lauca Formation.
Remains or traces of past living things preserved in rock.
A vent where hot gas and steam escape through cracks in volcanic ground.
A hot spring that periodically shoots jets of hot water and steam into the air.
An area with outstanding geological heritage managed for conservation, education and the sustainable development of local communities.
A place where geological features of scientific, educational, cultural or tourist value can be seen, and which should be protected.
Related to the Earth's internal heat. A geothermal field is an area where that heat warms groundwater.
A cold period when glaciers advance and cover large areas. The last one ended about 11,700 years ago.
A U-shaped valley carved by a glacier. Rivers, by contrast, carve V-shaped valleys.
A metamorphic rock with light and dark bands, formed under very high heat and pressure.
A light, coarse-grained intrusive rock rich in quartz and feldspar.
An intrusive rock between granite and diorite; very common in Chilean batholiths.
Rock formed by cooling magma or lava. It can be volcanic (at the surface) or intrusive (at depth).
A rock formed by the deposit of a gigantic pyroclastic flow: hot ash and pumice that weld together as they pile up.
Rock formed from magma that cooled below the surface, within other rocks.
Molten lava exposed inside a volcano's crater. Very few volcanoes in the world have one.
A volcanic mudflow: water mixed with ash and rock rushing down valleys. It forms when snow or glaciers melt, or when rain falls on ash.
Lava with a rough surface of sharp-edged blocks. The name comes from Hawaiian.
Lava with a smooth or rope-like surface. Also a Hawaiian term.
Pillow-shaped lava that forms when it cools quickly underwater.
A wide, shallow volcanic crater formed by explosions when magma meets groundwater.
Molten rock beneath the Earth's surface. When it reaches the surface it is called lava.
A metamorphic rock formed when limestone is transformed by heat and pressure.
Large animals that lived in the Pleistocene, such as mylodons, gomphotheres and American horses.
Rock transformed by heat and pressure without melting, such as marble, gneiss or schist.
A fragment of rock or metal from space that reaches the Earth's surface.
A Chilean protected-area category for places with unique natural features.
A Chilean protection category for sites of natural, scientific or scenic value.
A sphere of concentric mineral layers within an intrusive rock. Orbicular rocks are very rare worldwide.
The science that studies fossils and past life.
A Mesozoic marine reptile with a long neck and flippers; it was not a dinosaur.
A bend in rock layers caused by compression, without breaking them.
A column of hot material rising from the deep mantle that creates volcanoes, as in Easter Island or Hawaii.
A very light volcanic rock full of bubbles; some pieces float on water.
Rock and lava fragments thrown out in an explosive eruption, from fine ash to large bombs.
A feldspar mineral, white to gray, very common in volcanic and intrusive rocks.
Sernageomin's ranking of Chile's active volcanoes by the risk they pose to people and infrastructure.
Rock formed by the accumulation and compaction of particles (sand, mud) or the remains of organisms.
A basin covered with salt crusts, formed when water evaporates and leaves dissolved minerals behind.
A compound of silicon and oxygen; it makes up quartz and glass. Siliceous sinter is a silica crust that precipitates from hot springs.
A flat coastal surface carved by waves and later uplifted above sea level.
Movements of the plates and crust that raise mountains, fold rocks and cause earthquakes.
A light intrusive rock rich in plagioclase and quartz, similar to granite.
A fragment of another rock trapped in magma that later solidified; a 'foreign rock'.
A soft calcium sulfate mineral, common in salt flats and places where water evaporates.
